segments.title: Chương 162: Đi con đường của Tencent, để Tencent không còn đường đi
segments.content:
Chapter 165: Walk Tencent's Path, Leaving Tencent with No Path to Walk

Since he was the boss, he had to have a secretary.

Chen Guiliang now had an administrative secretary.

Her name was Hu Yuexia, 28 years old, a graduate of Beijing College of Finance and Commerce Management (a junior college), which had been renamed Beijing Vocational College of Finance and Commerce two years ago.

She was headhunted from Sohu by the newly hired HR, Wei Xiaokang, and was responsible for handling emails, screening phone calls, filing documents, taking meeting minutes, receiving visitors, and so on.

Chen Guiliang hadn't hired an executive assistant yet, so Hu Yuexia also had to handle some assistant duties.

"Mr. Chen, Mr. Liu from Pixel Soft has returned to Beijing. He said you can go see him anytime," Hu Yuexia said.

Chen Guiliang said, "Arrange for a car, I'll go over in the afternoon. And let them know as well."

The company had recently bought two cars.

One was a domestically produced Audi A4, used by any senior executive who needed to go out. It wasn't anyone's exclusive car.

The other was a Jinbei van, which could be used for transporting people or goods.

Before leaving Beijing, Chen Guiliang still had to make a trip to Changping to talk with Pixel Software Studio.

This was one of the top four game studios in the country, with *Blade & Sword* as its representative work.

At this time, Pixel Soft's office was located in the Changping Park of Zhongguancun. It was a rather remote location, more than 20 kilometers from Peking University. The only good thing one could say was that the air was decent.

They agreed to meet at three in the afternoon. Chen Guiliang didn't bring anyone and went alone in the Audi.

"Mr. Liu, I've arrived."

"Please wait a moment, I'll come down to get you."

A short while later, a man in his late twenties, wearing a crumpled T-shirt, came downstairs.

He was Liu Kun, the boss of Pixel Soft.

"Sorry for the sudden intrusion," Chen Guiliang said with a smile.

Liu Kun explained, "It's not that I'm putting on airs. I received a call from your company a few days ago, but I wasn't in Beijing at the time. I was busy negotiating a partnership with an agent from Taiwan."

"*Blade & Sword Online* has been sold to Taiwan?" Chen Guiliang asked.

"It has," Liu Kun said, too embarrassed to mention that the licensing fee wasn't much.

Chen Guiliang smiled, "Congratulations, congratulations."

Liu Kun invited Chen Guiliang for a tour of the company. To be honest, the place was quite shabby.

The core of the studio consisted of just 11 people. Without any outsourcing, they had made *Blade & Sword* in 8 months, and then spent another two years creating the online version.

Even now, while operating *Blade & Sword Online* themselves, the total number of full-time employees was less than 25.

No wonder the game's operation was so lackluster.

After showing Chen Guiliang around the company, Liu Kun asked, "Mr. Chen, are you interested in becoming an agent for *Blade & Sword Online*?"

"Is that possible?" Chen Guiliang asked back.

Liu Kun shook his head repeatedly, "We operate our own game."

Chen Guiliang thought to himself: And then you won't be able to keep operating it, and will be forced to let Sohu take over, only to find out that Sohu is also a坑货 (kēnghuò - a con or a cheat).

Chen Guiliang wasn't very interested in *Blade & Sword Online*. He had his eyes on Liu Kun's studio.

There weren't many teams in China that had their own self-developed game engine.

Moreover, the other major studios were not poachable.

Kingsoft was backed by Kingsoft Corporation.

The boss of Perfect World was a wealthy man himself.

Only the Pixel Software Studio before him was a guerilla force with no backing.

Chen Guiliang said, "I greatly admire Pixel Soft's team spirit and your passion for the gaming industry. I'm also a big fan of *Blade & Sword*. Is there any possibility of a partnership?"

Liu Kun refused outright, "We want to maintain our independence, free from any outside interference."

Chen Guiliang liked such purists, but only when not talking business.

"I also want to develop my own game engine. Could I borrow two people from your team?" Chen Guiliang tried a different approach.

With two senior members involved, Chen Guiliang could shorten his game engine development time by at least half a year!

Especially since the Pixel Soft team was skilled at rendering the impact of fighting games.

Liu Kun shook his head, "We're busy optimizing our engine. No one can be spared."

Sigh, not willing to sell, not willing to lend people.

Chen Guiliang said, "We can have a collaborative exchange. I'll lend you two people, and you lend me five, for a period of one and a half years. How about that? I'll cover the salaries of all seven people!"

"Is that really necessary?" Liu Kun still refused.

Chen Guiliang said, "The five people I'll give you are all top students from prestigious universities. They learn very quickly. They'll be up to speed in just a month, and will greatly improve your studio's efficiency."

Liu Kun was caught between laughter and tears, "I lend you two people to help you develop an engine and lead a team. And you send five people over to my place to steal my technology? You're taking all the benefits."

Chen Guiliang asked, "Do you think you can last long by going it alone? Your development capabilities are strong, but your business operations are too weak. The standalone version of *Blade & Sword* was so popular, what were the sales numbers?"

"It sold quite well," Liu Kun said.

Tens of thousands of copies sold was indeed quite good in 2002.

Chen Guiliang said, "Why don't you make a downloadable and installable version of *Blade & Sword*? I'll put it up for sale on the Game Science Interactive Entertainment platform. I don't know how many it will sell, but it should still generate some sales."

Liu Kun was tempted. "How do we split the revenue?"

"The platform only takes a 25% cut," Chen Guiliang said.

Game platforms usually take a 30% cut, but Chen Guiliang was willing to take less. This was mainly because the domestic single-player market was in such a dire state; platforms and developers should work together to grow the pie.

Liu Kun agreed immediately, "Deal."

Then he added, "But other collaborations still need consideration."

"Is Pixel Soft open to investment?" Chen Guiliang asked.

Without a second thought, Liu Kun said, "No."

So obstinate!

Chen Guiliang said, "Let's stick with the collaborative exchange then. A swap of 2 and 5 employees, I'll pay all seven salaries. But let's shorten the time to half a year. And I'll give *Blade & Sword Online* a 50% discount on banner ads on Xiaonei.com for half a month."

ByteDance and Game Science had already split, so Game Science would have to pay for this 50% discount.

The company developing the game engine was, of course, also Game Science!

Liu Kun didn't directly refuse this time. Instead, he said, "I can license the Blade & Sword engine to you for a fee. That way, you won't have to develop your own."

"I want to make an engine for a side-scrolling game, with graphics similar to old arcade games," Chen Guiliang said. "There aren't any suitable commercial engines on the market right now, so I have to develop it myself. Your engine isn't a perfect fit either, but it's similar enough to shorten my development cycle."

Liu Kun's eyes lit up. "A game like an arcade game? Single-player or online?"

"Online," Chen Guiliang said.

"Alright, I agree. I'll lend you two partners who are in charge of physics collision and rendering optimization!" Liu Kun found this very novel.

Chen Guiliang was lending him people to lead his teams, and his own people could also gain relevant experience.

Moreover, Liu Kun was quite looking forward to this kind of side-scrolling arcade-style online game.

What was Chen Guiliang trying to do?

Of course, it was to make a game similar to *Dungeon Fighter Online*.

*Dungeon Fighter Online* had already been made by the Koreans and would enter open beta in two months.

But it was still a long way from entering China.

In the other timeline, because there were too many Chinese companies wanting to license the game, the creators of *Dungeon Fighter Online* took the opportunity to drive up the price.

One after another, Chinese agents took turns negotiating with the Koreans for over a year, all scared off by the high price the Koreans were demanding.

Procrastinating like this, a game that went into open beta in 2005 was only secured by Tencent in December 2007, and it took until March 2008 for closed beta testing in China.

As for the open beta, that would have to wait until June 2008.

In other words, a full three years from now!

Three years was enough time for Chen Guiliang to make one himself, and that included developing his own game engine.

Chen Guiliang could even go and disrupt the situation by intentionally offering a high price to compete with Tencent. Given the Koreans' money-grubbing nature, with Chen Guiliang's meddling, they might even drag it out for another half a year before selling to Tencent.

A three-and-a-half-year delay, and the day lily would be cold.
